segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he came back into Capernaum after some days, it was heard that he was at home.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And so many gathered that there was no longer any room, not even around the door, and he was speaking the word to them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And some people came bringing him a paralyzed man, carried by four men.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Unable to bring him to Jesus because of the crowd, they removed the roof above where he was, and after digging through it they lowered the mat on which the paralyzed man was lying.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Seeing their faith, Jesus said to the paralyzed man,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Child, your sins are forgiven.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now some of the scribes were sitting there, reasoning in their hearts,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Why does this man speak like this? He is blaspheming! Who can forgive sins except God alone?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At once Jesus, perceiving in his spirit that they were reasoning this way within themselves, said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Why are you reasoning these things in your hearts?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Which is easier: to say to the paralyzed man, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Get up, pick up your mat, and walk’?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins—”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: he said to the paralyzed man,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I say to you, get up, pick up your mat, and go to your home.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he got up, at once picked up the mat, and went out in front of them all, so that all were astonished and glorified God, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “We have never seen anything like this!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He went out again beside the sea, and the whole crowd kept coming to him, and he was teaching them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As he passed by, he saw Levi son of Alphaeus sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Follow me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he got up and followed him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And it happened that he was reclining at table in his house, and many tax collectors and sinners were reclining with Jesus and his disciples, for there were many of them, and they were following him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the scribes of the Pharisees saw that he was eating with the sinners and tax collectors, they said to his disciples,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Why does he eat with the tax collectors and sinners?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Hearing this, Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick. I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now John’s disciples and the Pharisees were fasting. And people came and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Why do John’s disciples and the disciples of the Pharisees fast, but your disciples do not fast?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “The wedding guests cannot fast while the bridegroom is with them, can they? As long as they have the bridegroom with them, they cannot fast.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast, on that day.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: No one sews a patch of unshrunk cloth onto an old garment. Otherwise the patch pulls away from it, the new from the old, and a worse tear results.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And no one puts new wine into old wineskins. Otherwise the wine will burst the skins, and the wine is lost, and the skins too. Instead, new wine into new wineskins.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It happened that on the Sabbath he was passing through the grainfields, and as they made their way his disciples began to pick the heads of grain.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the Pharisees said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Look, why are they doing on the Sabbath what is not permitted?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Have you never read what David did when he was in need and hungry, he and those with him—

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: how he entered the house of God in the time of Abiathar the high priest and ate the loaves of presentation, which no one is permitted to eat except the priests, and gave some also to those who were with him?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “The Sabbath was made for people, not people for the Sabbath.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath.”

notes.note: Village houses in Galilee typically had flat roofs of wooden beams covered with branches and packed clay, reached by an outside stair or ladder. Such a roof could be dug through, which is the verb Mark uses, and repaired afterwards.

The Greek word means 'child' without reference to sex and is used here as an affectionate form of address to an adult. Most English versions have 'Son', which fits the man but uses a different word from the one Mark chose; some recent versions also have 'Child'.

The traditional word is kept, but these were not copyists. In the Gospels the term means trained experts in the Law of Moses, who taught it and gave rulings on its application. Some translations render it 'teachers of the law' or 'legal experts'.

In Semitic idiom 'a son of man' means simply a human being, but in the Gospels 'the Son of Man' is Jesus's characteristic way of referring to himself. Many scholars see behind it the figure 'like a son of man' who is given authority in Daniel 7:13–14, though how much of that background is in view in each saying is debated. Some interpreters also take the first half of this verse as Mark's aside to the reader, not Jesus's words to the scribes.

In Galilee these were mainly collectors of tolls and customs duties on goods in transit, working under contractors for Herod Antipas. They were widely regarded as dishonest and, because of their trade and contacts, were classed socially with notorious sinners.

The Greek does not say whose house this is. Most interpreters take it to be Levi's, as Luke 5:29 says explicitly, but the wording allows Jesus's own home in Capernaum (compare verse 1). The translation leaves the pronoun as open as the Greek does.

Greek has a single word-family where English has two: the same word means both 'righteous' and 'just', and its noun both 'righteousness' and 'justice'. Here it describes people who are in the right before God. Whether Jesus uses it of his critics straightforwardly or with irony is debated.

notes.traditional: the children of the bridechamber; the wedding guests
notes.note: Literally 'the sons of the bridal chamber', a Semitic idiom for those who belong to the wedding party, either the guests in general or the bridegroom's attendants in particular. A wedding feast was a time of celebration at which fasting would have been out of place.

notes.phrase: began to pick the heads of grain
notes.note: Picking grain by hand while walking through another person's field was allowed (Deuteronomy 23:25), so the objection is not to theft. The Pharisees' complaint is that picking counted as reaping, a form of work forbidden on the Sabbath.

notes.phrase: in the time of Abiathar the high priest
notes.traditional: in the days of Abiathar the high priest
notes.note: In 1 Samuel 21:1–6 the priest who gives David the bread is Ahimelech, the father of Abiathar. The usual rendering, followed here, takes the phrase as a time reference, which leaves a discrepancy that scholars explain in various ways. A minority take it to mean 'in the passage about Abiathar', as a way of locating the story in the scroll. Matthew and Luke omit the phrase, as do a few manuscripts of Mark.

notes.traditional: the bread of the Presence; the showbread
notes.note: The Greek phrase, taken from the Septuagint, means the loaves that are 'set out', that is, the twelve loaves placed before God in the sanctuary each Sabbath (Leviticus 24:5–9). 'Bread of the Presence' renders the underlying Hebrew expression, not the Greek. Both refer to the same loaves.

The Greek word here means human beings in general, so 'people' is used in place of the traditional 'man'. The cost is that English no longer shows the verbal link with 'the Son of Man' in the next verse, where the same Greek word appears. Some scholars think the saying originally meant that humanity is lord of the Sabbath; most hold that Mark intends it as a claim about Jesus.
